properties.name: The unreachable-vocabulary baseline is split by intent: 14 holes, 15 written by an operation, 13 unused — and the count can be read as a to-do list again
properties.rationale:
Anthony asked whether to address the 43 unreachable properties and the honest answer was no, not as a block — about two thirds of them are correctly unreachable and a parameter for them would be a forgery hazard rather than a feature. But saying that in a reply would have left the number wrong for the next reader, so the split belongs in the artifact rather than in the conversation.

IT IS THE SAME FUSED-QUESTION DEFECT ONE LAYER ALONG, and that is the reason this was worth doing before the holes themselves. Earlier the same day this instrument was fixed for fusing REACHABILITY with ADOPTION. It was still fusing reachability with INTENT: it could tell that nothing writes a property and not whether anything should. Each fix answered its own question correctly and left the next one folded in behind it.

WHAT IS NOT DONE: the 14 holes are not filled. That is the next piece of work and it is now a list somebody can act on rather than a number that overstates itself by two thirds. Three of the 14 belong to types with no constructor at all, which is a decision about whether those types should be user-writable and is Anthony's rather than an agent's.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
The baseline was a flat list of 43 property names, and Anthony asked whether they should all be fixed. Reading them showed the count conflated two opposite things, so the number could not be acted on: a HOLE that somebody wants filled, and a property an OPERATION writes where a caller parameter would be actively wrong. Offering a parameter for a creation timestamp or a computed mirror hash lets a caller forge a fact the system computes.

EVERY ENTRY NOW CARRIES A KIND AND A REASON A READER CAN DISAGREE WITH, and a machine_written one names the operation in `written_by` — a claim that something else writes it is unfalsifiable without naming what. The split, evidence-based rather than guessed: each property was traced to the code that sets it, per TYPE rather than per name, because property names are shared across types and a bare name grep over-attributes.

14 HOLE: Actor.actor_type and .description (no constructor exists at all), Capability.is_entry_point / .is_exit_point / .tier, Component.tier, Constraint.concern / .priority, Flow.tier, Fragment.content_ref / .note_kind, Interface.spec, Project.decomposition_levels, Requirement.concern. Project.decomposition_levels is the sharpest: hierarchy.rs reads the design's own ladder on every level check and no tool can set it.

15 WRITTEN BY AN OPERATION: the drift-event trio, the four mirror-coordinate fields, the two snapshot payload fields, the two provenance-fragment fields, the two question-phrasing fields, the artifact's last-confirmed date, and the decision's alternatives.

13 UNUSED: six *_created_at / captured_at fields nothing carries, because THE CORE TAKES NO CLOCK by design, plus seven others declared and never written.

ONE WAS NEITHER, AND THE INSTRUMENT WAS SIMPLY WRONG ABOUT IT. Component.purpose reported as unreachable while add_component writes it under a parameter spelled `description`. That is a false finding, not a deliberate state, so the fix is an ALIASED map the instrument reads rather than a classification excusing it — the docstring had warned about the name-mismatch class since the first version and nothing enumerated an instance. The list is 42 now, not 43.

`--update-baseline` PRESERVES classifications and INVENTS NONE: a new entry lands UNCLASSIFIED and `--check` keeps failing until a person says which kind it is and why. Refreshing the file must not be a way to make the question go away. Proven by dropping an entry and re-running both modes.
